claim: DNA polymerase I (Pol I) from Escherichia coli is a key enzyme involved in lagging-strand replication and base excision repair.
source: DNA polymerase I (Pol I) from Escherichia coli, a key enzyme involved in lagging-strand replication and base excision repair.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: A DNA substrate can spontaneously transfer between polymerase and 5' nuclease domains during a single encounter with Pol I.
source: We show that a DNA substrate can spontaneously transfer between polymerase and 5' nuclease domains during a single encounter with Pol I.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by smFRET experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The flexibly tethered 5' nuclease domain adopts different positions within Pol I-DNA complexes, depending on the nature of the DNA substrate.
source: Additionally, we show that the flexibly tethered 5' nuclease domain adopts different positions within Pol I-DNA complexes, depending on the nature of the DNA substrate.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by smFRET experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: DNA polymerase I contains three distinct enzymatic activities: a DNA-dependent 5'–3' polymerase (pol), a proofreading 3'–5' exonuclease (exo) and a 5' nuclease (5' nuc).
source: DNA polymerase I (Pol I), a key enzyme involved in DNA replication and repair in Escherichia coli (Makiela-Dzbenska et al., 2009; Imai et al., 2007; Patel et al., 2001), contains three distinct enzymatic activities in a single 928 residue polypeptide: a DNA-dependent 5'–3' polymerase (pol), a proofreading 3'–5' exonuclease (exo) and a 5' nuclease (5' nuc) (Kelley and Joyce, 1983; Setlow and Kornberg, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: The pol and exo activities are contained in separate domains, which together comprise the main body of the enzyme.
source: The pol and exo activities are contained in separate domains, which together comprise the main body of the enzyme, whereas the 5' nuc activity is located in an independent domain that is tethered to the body by an unstructured 16 amino acid (aa) peptide linker.
evidence: This is based on established structural knowledge of Pol I.

claim: The 5' nuc domain is tethered to the body of Pol I by an unstructured 16 amino acid peptide linker.
source: The pol and exo activities are contained in separate domains, which together comprise the main body of the enzyme, whereas the 5' nuc activity is located in an independent domain that is tethered to the body by an unstructured 16 amino acid (aa) peptide linker.
evidence: This is based on established structural knowledge of Pol I.

claim: The 5' nuc domain is related to the flap endonuclease (FEN) family of structure-specific DNA nucleases.
source: The 5' nuc domain is related to the flap endonuclease (FEN) family of structure-specific DNA nucleases (Harrington and Lieber, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Pol I plays an important role in lagging strand DNA replication in E. coli.
source: Pol I plays an important role in lagging strand DNA replication in E. coli (Balakrishnan and Bambara, 2013; Okazaki et al., 1971).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: During lagging strand replication, short RNA primers anneal to the lagging strand and are extended by DNA primase, producing fused RNA-DNA strands (Okazaki fragments).
source: During this complex process, short RNA primers anneal to the lagging strand and are extended by DNA primase, producing fused RNA-DNA strands (Okazaki fragments).
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of Okazaki fragment formation.

claim: The nascent DNA portion of Okazaki fragments is extended by Pol I until the growing strand encounters another Okazaki fragment lying downstream, displacing the 5' end and forming an RNA flap.
source: The nascent DNA portion is subsequently extended by Pol I, until the growing strand encounters another Okazaki fragment lying downstream, displacing the 5' end and forming an RNA flap.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of Okazaki fragment processing.

claim: The 5' nuc activity of Pol I cleaves the RNA flap, generating a nicked DNA substrate that is subsequently sealed by a DNA ligase.
source: The 5' nuc activity of Pol I then cleaves the RNA flap, generating a nicked DNA substrate that is subsequently sealed by a DNA ligase (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A showing the process and is established knowledge.

claim: The same processing steps performed during Okazaki fragment maturation are also performed by Pol I during DNA base excision repair, except the displaced strand is composed of DNA.
source: The same processing steps are also performed by Pol I during DNA base excision repair, in which case the displaced strand is composed of DNA (Imai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Pol I must achieve an appropriate balance between the pol and 5' nuc activities to generate a nicked duplex product that can be sealed by a DNA ligase.
source: During either Okazaki fragment processing or base excision repair, Pol I must achieve an appropriate balance between the pol and 5' nuc activities in order to generate a nicked duplex product that can subsequently be sealed by a DNA ligase (Mortusewicz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation and represents established understanding.

claim: Excessive pol activity can generate long downstream 5' flaps that are difficult to cleave.
source: Excessive pol activity can generate long downstream 5' flaps that are difficult to cleave (Reha-Krantz, 2010), while excessive 5' nuc activity can result in extended regions of single-stranded DNA that are prone to breakage (Zheng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Excessive 5' nuc activity can result in extended regions of single-stranded DNA that are prone to breakage.
source: Excessive pol activity can generate long downstream 5' flaps that are difficult to cleave (Reha-Krantz, 2010), while excessive 5' nuc activity can result in extended regions of single-stranded DNA that are prone to breakage (Zheng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Either excessive pol activity or excessive 5' nuc activity is deleterious to genomic integrity and cellular survival.
source: Either outcome is deleterious to genomic integrity and cellular survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the preceding statements about the consequences of imbalanced activities.

claim: 5' flap cleavage is performed by the same Pol I molecule that extended the primer.
source: A previous biochemical study suggests that 5' flap cleavage is performed by the same Pol I molecule that extended the primer (Xu et al., 2000), indicating a high degree of functional coordination.
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The structural and physical basis for functional coordination in Pol I is unknown.
source: However, the structural and physical basis for this coordination is unknown, since crystal structures of Pol I engaged with DNA substrates via the pol or 5' nuc domains have not been reported to date.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Crystal structures of Pol I engaged with DNA substrates via the pol or 5' nuc domains have not been reported.
source: However, the structural and physical basis for this coordination is unknown, since crystal structures of Pol I engaged with DNA substrates via the pol or 5' nuc domains have not been reported to date.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The structure of Taq polymerase bound to DNA reveals that the primer 3' terminus is located within the palm region of the pol domain, while the 5' nuc domain is extended away from the enzyme core.
source: However, the structure of the Pol I homolog Taq polymerase bound to DNA (Eom et al., 1996) reveals that the primer 3' terminus is located within the palm region of the pol domain, while the 5' nuc domain is extended away from the enzyme core (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation and Figure 1B showing the crystal structure.

claim: The structure of human FEN1 in complex with a DNA substrate provides a model for how the 5' nuc domain of Pol I engages a DNA substrate.
source: Moreover, the structure of human FEN1, which is homologous to the 5' nuc domain of Pol I, in complex with a DNA substrate provides a model for how the 5' nuc domain of Pol I engages a DNA substrate (Tsutakawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The FEN1-DNA structure shows a single unpaired base at the primer 3' terminus inserted into a pocket of FEN1.
source: The structure shows a single unpaired base at the primer 3' terminus inserted into a pocket of FEN1 and a region of extended contacts between the protein and the sugar-phosphate backbones of both strands of the downstream DNA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation and Figure 1C showing the structure.

claim: The FEN1-DNA structure shows a region of extended contacts between the protein and the sugar-phosphate backbones of both strands of the downstream DNA.
source: The structure shows a single unpaired base at the primer 3' terminus inserted into a pocket of FEN1 and a region of extended contacts between the protein and the sugar-phosphate backbones of both strands of the downstream DNA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation and Figure 1C showing the structure.

claim: The pol and 5' nuc binding modes of Pol I must differ significantly.
source: These structures of homologous enzymes suggest that the pol and 5' nuc binding modes of Pol I must differ significantly, raising questions about how the enzyme switches from one mode of activity to another.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural information about homologous enzymes.

claim: Theoretical modeling suggests that the 5' nuc domain flips by ∼180° and adopts a position above the fingers and thumb subdomains within the enzyme core during the transition from pol to 5' nuc activity.
source: Theoretical modeling of the transition from pol to 5' nuc activity in Pol I, starting from the extended enzyme conformation shown in Figure 1B, suggests that the 5' nuc domain flips by ∼180° and adopts a position above the fingers and thumb subdomains within the enzyme core (Xie and Sayers, 2011), facilitating interactions with the primer terminal base and a downstream DNA flap.
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation describing theoretical modeling.

claim: The primer terminal base must detach from the pol domain in order to insert into the 5' nuc domain.
source: Additionally, it is likely that the primer terminal base must detach from the pol domain in order to insert into the 5' nuc domain, as seen in the FEN1-DNA structure (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the FEN1-DNA structure.

claim: The hypothetical movements of the DNA substrate and 5' nuc domain have not been observed experimentally.
source: However, these hypothetical movements of the DNA substrate and 5' nuc domain have not been observed experimentally.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: smFRET has been previously applied to Klenow fragment (KF), which is derived from Pol I by removal of the 5' nuc domain.
source: The smFRET method has been previously applied to Klenow fragment (KF), which is derived from Pol I by removal of the 5' nuc domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KF.

claim: Previous smFRET studies have monitored DNA synthesis by KF.
source: These studies have monitored DNA synthesis by KF (Christian et al., 2009), detected nucleotide-induced conformational transitions within KF (Santoso et al., 2010; Berezhna et al., 2012; Hohlbein et al., 2013), monitored a DNA primer switching between the pol and exo sites of KF (Lamichhane et al., 2013) and established a structural model of a DNA substrate bound to KF (Craggs et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Previous smFRET studies have detected nucleotide-induced conformational transitions within KF.
source: These studies have monitored DNA synthesis by KF (Christian et al., 2009), detected nucleotide-induced conformational transitions within KF (Santoso et al., 2010; Berezhna et al., 2012; Hohlbein et al., 2013), monitored a DNA primer switching between the pol and exo sites of KF (Lamichhane et al., 2013) and established a structural model of a DNA substrate bound to KF (Craggs et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Previous smFRET studies have monitored a DNA primer switching between the pol and exo sites of KF.
source: These studies have monitored DNA synthesis by KF (Christian et al., 2009), detected nucleotide-induced conformational transitions within KF (Santoso et al., 2010; Berezhna et al., 2012; Hohlbein et al., 2013), monitored a DNA primer switching between the pol and exo sites of KF (Lamichhane et al., 2013) and established a structural model of a DNA substrate bound to KF (Craggs et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Previous smFRET studies have established a structural model of a DNA substrate bound to KF.
source: These studies have monitored DNA synthesis by KF (Christian et al., 2009), detected nucleotide-induced conformational transitions within KF (Santoso et al., 2010; Berezhna et al., 2012; Hohlbein et al., 2013), monitored a DNA primer switching between the pol and exo sites of KF (Lamichhane et al., 2013) and established a structural model of a DNA substrate bound to KF (Craggs et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: smFRET has not yet been applied to full-length Pol I.
source: However, smFRET has not yet been applied to full-length Pol I, or any other DNA polymerase containing a 5' nuc activity.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: The fractional populations and dwell times of DNA species engaging the pol and 5' nuc domains vary according to the nature of the DNA substrate.
source: In this study, we have developed an smFRET system to identify separate subpopulations of DNA engaging the pol and 5' nuc domains of Pol I, revealing how the fractional populations and dwell times of each species vary according to the nature of the DNA substrate.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The 5' nuc domain undergoes a large positional shift in order to interact with a downstream DNA strand.
source: We have also implemented a complementary smFRET system to probe the location of the flexibly tethered 5' nuc domain, revealing that this domain undergoes a large positional shift in order to interact with a downstream DNA strand.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: DNA substrates can switch between the pol and 5' nuc domains during a single encounter with Pol I.
source: Importantly, using both smFRET systems, we demonstrate that DNA substrates can switch between the pol and 5' nuc domains during a single encounter with Pol I.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: A base located within the primer strand was labelled with an Alexa Fluor 488 (A488) FRET donor and Pol I was labeled at position 550 in the thumb region with a complementary Alexa Fluor 594 (A594) FRET acceptor.
source: A base located within the primer strand was labelled with an Alexa Fluor 488 (A488) FRET donor and Pol I was labeled at position 550 in the thumb region with a complementary Alexa Fluor 594 (A594) FRET acceptor (Figure 3A and Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the first FRET labeling scheme.

claim: The Pol I construct contained C262S and C907S mutations to remove the two native cysteines.
source: To achieve site-specific labeling of Pol I, the two native cysteines were removed via C262S and C907S mutations, and a single cysteine was introduced at the desired labeling site via a K550C mutation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for protein labeling.

claim: The Pol I construct contained D424A and D116A mutations to eliminate 3'–5' exonuclease and 5' nuclease activities, respectively.
source: The Pol I construct also contained D424A and D116A mutations to eliminate 3'–5' exonuclease and 5' nuclease activities, respectively (Derbyshire et al., 1991; Xu et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by literature citations.

claim: During each encounter between Pol I and DNA, the FRET efficiency alternates between two distinct levels at ∼0.8 or ∼0.6 efficiency.
source: During the binding periods, the FRET efficiency alternates between two distinct levels at ∼0.8 or ∼0.6 efficiency.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Two distinct bound states are sufficient to account for all data sets from multiple FRET trajectories analyzed globally using a Hidden Markov model.
source: Multiple FRET trajectories for each DNA substrate interacting with Pol I were analyzed globally using a Hidden Markov model, confirming that two distinct bound states are sufficient to account for all data sets.
evidence: This is based on Hidden Markov modeling of the experimental data.

claim: A state at 0.8 FRET efficiency was previously observed for DNA primer/templates interacting with KF and was attributed to DNA engaging the pol domain.
source: A state at 0.8 FRET efficiency was previously observed for DNA primer/templates interacting with KF (same donor and acceptor labeling sites as here) and was attributed to DNA engaging the pol domain (Lamichhane et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The 0.8 FRET state observed in Pol I is attributed to DNA engaging the pol domain within Pol I (state P).
source: Since KF is identical to the main core of Pol I, the 0.8 FRET state observed here is also attributed to DNA engaging the pol domain within Pol I (state P).
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between KF and Pol I core.

claim: The L361A mutation has little effect on the 0.6 FRET population for the mixed flap and downstream flap substrates.
source: The L361A mutation has little effect on the 0.6 FRET population for the mixed flap and downstream flap substrates (compare top and middle rows in Figure 3C), indicating that this state does not arise from binding of these DNAs to the exo domain.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For the double-flap substrate, the presence of the L361A mutation decreased the population of the 0.6 FRET state by 15%.
source: However, for the double-flap substrate, the presence of the L361A mutation decreased the population of the 0.6 FRET state by 15% (Figure 3C), suggesting that this state arises, in part, from binding of the DNA to the exo domain.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A primer/template substrate containing a terminal mismatch exhibited a state at 0.6 FRET efficiency when bound to Pol I, and this state was completely eliminated with a L361A mutation within Pol I.
source: Consistent with this, a primer/template substrate containing the same terminal mismatch (Appendix 1—table 1) exhibited a state at 0.6 FRET efficiency when bound to Pol I, and this state was completely eliminated with a L361A mutation within Pol I Figure 3—figure supplement 2, confirming that mismatched DNA can engage the exo domain within Pol I.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mismatched DNA can engage the exo domain within Pol I.
source: Consistent with this, a primer/template substrate containing the same terminal mismatch (Appendix 1—table 1) exhibited a state at 0.6 FRET efficiency when bound to Pol I, and this state was completely eliminated with a L361A mutation within Pol I Figure 3—figure supplement 2, confirming that mismatched DNA can engage the exo domain within Pol I.
evidence: This is confirmed by the experimental data.

claim: The 0.6 FRET population is not observed for any of the DNA substrates in the presence of KF.
source: Notably, the 0.6 FRET population is not observed for any of the DNA substrates in the presence of KF (Figure 3C, bottom row).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The 0.6 FRET state arises primarily from DNA engaging the 5' nuc domain of Pol I (state N).
source: Together, these observations indicate that the 0.6 FRET state arises primarily from DNA engaging the 5' nuc domain of Pol I (state N).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations with KF and L361A mutants.

claim: In the case of the double flap substrate, the 0.6 FRET state also reflects a small (15%) population engaging the exo domain of Pol I (state E).
source: In the case of the double flap substrate, the 0.6 FRET state also reflects a small (15%) population engaging the exo domain of Pol I (state E).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data with L361A mutant.

claim: The presence of the downstream strand in the double flap substrate inhibits binding of DNA to the exo domain and/or favors binding to the 5' nuc domain.
source: Interestingly, this population is significantly less than observed for the primer/template containing the same terminal mismatch (53%, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that the presence of the downstream strand in the double flap substrate inhibits binding of DNA to the exo domain and/or favors binding to the 5' nuc domain.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the populations in different substrates.

claim: The Förster radius in state N is similar to that in state P.
source: Photophysical control experiments indicate that the Förster radius in state N is similar to that in state P (Appendix 4), indicating that the lower FRET efficiency of state N is due to physical movement of the DNA substrate and/or thumb subdomain.
evidence: This is based on photophysical control experiments.

claim: The lower FRET efficiency of state N is due to physical movement of the DNA substrate and/or thumb subdomain.
source: Photophysical control experiments indicate that the Förster radius in state N is similar to that in state P (Appendix 4), indicating that the lower FRET efficiency of state N is due to physical movement of the DNA substrate and/or thumb subdomain.
evidence: This is inferred from the photophysical control experiments.

claim: The thumb subdomain is a rigid structural element within Pol I and KF.
source: However, since the thumb subdomain is a rigid structural element within Pol I and KF, it is likely that the FRET change is actually due to movement of the DNA substrate.
evidence: This is based on established structural knowledge.

claim: The FRET change from state P to state N is likely due to movement of the DNA substrate.
source: However, since the thumb subdomain is a rigid structural element within Pol I and KF, it is likely that the FRET change is actually due to movement of the DNA substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the rigidity of the thumb subdomain.

claim: The change in FRET efficiency from 0.8 to 0.6 corresponds to a lengthening of the donor-acceptor distance of ∼7 Å.
source: The change in FRET efficiency from 0.8 to 0.6 corresponds to a lengthening of the donor-acceptor distance of ∼7 Å (Appendix 4).
evidence: This is calculated from the FRET efficiency change.

claim: The DNA must detach from the pol domain in order for the primer 3' terminus to reach either the 5' nuc domain or the exo domain.
source: This movement of the upstream DNA duplex is similar for states N and E, indicating that the DNA must detach from the pol domain in order for the primer 3' terminus to reach either the 5' nuc domain or the exo domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar FRET efficiencies of states N and E.

claim: State N is highly populated for the double-flap substrate (59%, after accounting for the population of state E).
source: State N is highly populated for the double-flap substrate (59%, after accounting for the population of state E, Figure 3C, top left) and mixed-flap substrate (54%, Figure 3C, top middle).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: State N is highly populated for the mixed-flap substrate (54%).
source: State N is highly populated for the double-flap substrate (59%, after accounting for the population of state E, Figure 3C, top left) and mixed-flap substrate (54%, Figure 3C, top middle).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Double-flap and mixed-flap substrates contain or can form double-flap structures that are the preferred substrates for the 5' nuc activity of Pol I.
source: Both DNAs contain or can form double-flap structures that are the preferred substrates for the 5' nuc activity of Pol I (Xu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: State N is least populated with the downstream flap substrate (23%).
source: In contrast, state N is least populated with the downstream flap substrate (23%, Figure 3C, top right).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pol I can engage DNA via one domain (pol or 5' nuc), dissociate into bulk solution, and subsequently rebind using the other domain.
source: These results imply that Pol I can engage DNA via one domain (pol or 5' nuc), dissociate into bulk solution, and subsequently rebind using the other domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the transition density plots shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Dissociation and rebinding provide one pathway for transfer of DNA substrates between pol and 5' nuc domains (intermolecular transfer).
source: Dissociation and rebinding provide one pathway for transfer of DNA substrates between pol and 5' nuc domains (intermolecular transfer).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Frequent transitions between states P and N occur that do not show a measurable pause in a zero-FRET state.
source: In addition, we observe frequent transitions between states P and N that do not show a measurable pause in a zero-FRET state (examples are shown in Figure 3B, between ∼8s and ∼10s and in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: Direct transitions between states P and N give rise to prominent cross peaks between 0.6 and 0.8 FRET states in the TDPs.
source: These direct transitions give rise to prominent cross peaks between 0.6 and 0.8 FRET states in the TDPs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A single Pol I molecule is bound to DNA under the conditions of the experiments.
source: We conclude that a single Pol I molecule is bound to DNA under the conditions of our experiments, ruling out the second scenario described above.
evidence: This is based on stoichiometry analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Transfer from the pol domain to 5' nuc domain is fastest for the double flap substrate and slowest for the downstream flap substrate.
source: Transfer from the pol domain to 5' nuc domain is fastest for the double flap substrate and slowest for the downstream flap substrate (Figure 3E, Appendix 3—table 3).
evidence: This is observed in the kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The rates of dissociation from the pol domain are similar for each substrate.
source: In contrast, the rates of dissociation from the pol domain are similar for each substrate (Appendix 3—table 3).
evidence: This is observed in the kinetic analysis.

claim: Transfer from the pol domain to the 5' nuc domain is kinetically distinct from overall dissociation from the pol domain.
source: Hence, transfer from the pol domain to the 5' nuc domain is kinetically distinct from overall dissociation from the pol domain, emphasizing the intramolecular nature of the process.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic analysis.

claim: The downstream flap substrate exhibits the fastest transfer from the 5' nuc domain to the pol domain.
source: The downstream flap substrate exhibits the fastest transfer.
evidence: This is observed in the kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Transfer of the double flap substrate from the 5' nuc domain to the pol domain is much slower than the downstream flap substrate.
source: In contrast, transfer of the double flap substrate is much slower, showing the importance of the unpaired primer base for stable engagement with the 5' nuc domain.
evidence: This is observed in the kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The unpaired primer base is important for stable engagement with the 5' nuc domain.
source: In contrast, transfer of the double flap substrate is much slower, showing the importance of the unpaired primer base for stable engagement with the 5' nuc domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic analysis.

claim: The unpaired primer base is sequestered in a binding pocket in the FEN1 structure, making contacts with a network of surrounding protein residues.
source: The structure of FEN1 (homologous to the 5' nuc domain of Pol I) with DNA reveals that the unpaired primer base is sequestered in a binding pocket, making contacts with a network of surrounding protein residues (Tsutakawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: A similar arrangement in Pol I would account for the prolonged residence time of DNA in state N and the slow return to state P.
source: A similar arrangement in Pol I would account for the prolonged residence time of DNA in state N and the slow return to state P.
evidence: This is inferred from the FEN1 structure and the kinetic data.

claim: A DNA substrate containing only primer and template strands exhibits a single FRET state at ∼0.8 efficiency, corresponding to state P, while interacting with Pol I.
source: This substrate exhibits a single FRET state at ∼0.8 efficiency, corresponding to state P, while interacting with Pol I (Figure 4A and B, bottom panels).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: No cross peaks are observed in the TDP for the primer/template substrate.
source: Likewise, no cross peaks are observed in the TDP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: State N is absent for the primer/template substrate, showing that the downstream DNA must be in duplex form to engage the 5' nuc domain.
source: State N is absent in this case, showing that the downstream DNA must be in duplex form to engage the 5' nuc domain and promote movement of the upstream DNA out of the pol domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: DNA substrates containing a nick or single-stranded gaps reveal reversible transitions between ∼0.6 and ∼0.8 FRET states when interacting with Pol I.
source: These substrates reveal reversible transitions between ∼0.6 and ∼0.8 FRET states when interacting with Pol I (Figure 4A, upper three panels), similar to the substrates containing 5' flaps.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The populations of state N for the nicked and single-nucleotide gap substrates (26% and 23%, respectively) are similar to the downstream flap substrate (23%).
source: The populations of state N for the nicked and single-nucleotide gap substrates (26% and 23%, respectively, Figure 4B) are similar to the downstream flap substrate (23%, Figure 3C), indicating that the presence of a downstream strand is sufficient to engage the 5' nuc domain, regardless of whether that strand contains a 5' flap or not.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 4B.

claim: The presence of a downstream strand is sufficient to engage the 5' nuc domain, regardless of whether that strand contains a 5' flap or not.
source: The populations of state N for the nicked and single-nucleotide gap substrates (26% and 23%, respectively, Figure 4B) are similar to the downstream flap substrate (23%, Figure 3C), indicating that the presence of a downstream strand is sufficient to engage the 5' nuc domain, regardless of whether that strand contains a 5' flap or not.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of state N populations.

claim: The 5' nuc domain can engage a downstream strand even when it is separated from the primer strand by a 4nt gap.
source: Moreover, the 5' nuc domain can engage a downstream strand even when it is separated from the primer strand by a 4nt gap (Figure 4A and B), which is likely a consequence of the flexible 16 aa linker tethering the 5' nuc domain to the body of the enzyme.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The ability of the 5' nuc domain to engage a downstream strand separated by a 4nt gap is likely a consequence of the flexible 16 aa linker tethering the 5' nuc domain to the body of the enzyme.
source: Moreover, the 5' nuc domain can engage a downstream strand even when it is separated from the primer strand by a 4nt gap (Figure 4A and B), which is likely a consequence of the flexible 16 aa linker tethering the 5' nuc domain to the body of the enzyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural features of Pol I.

claim: The flexibility of the single-stranded gap region could facilitate docking of the 5' nuc domain with the downstream DNA strand.
source: The flexibility of the single-stranded gap region could also facilitate docking of the 5' nuc domain with the downstream DNA strand.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism.

claim: A gapped DNA substrate can transfer reversibly between pol and 5' nuc domains during a single encounter with Pol I.
source: The presence of prominent cross peaks in the TDP shows that a gapped DNA substrate can transfer reversibly between pol and 5' nuc domains during a single encounter with Pol I (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Transfer from the pol domain to the 5' nuc domain becomes progressively slower as the gap size increases.
source: Transfer from the pol domain to the 5' nuc domain becomes progressively slower as the gap size increases (Figure 4D and Appendix 3—table 5).
evidence: This is observed in the kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Return of all DNAs from the 5' nuc domain to the pol domain is more rapid than transfer from pol to 5' nuc domain.
source: Return of all DNAs from the 5' nuc domain to the pol domain is more rapid (Figure 4D and Appendix 3—table 5).
evidence: This is observed in the kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4D.
